newsitem.title: USA: Unpredictable weather threatens U.S. shuttle launch.
newsitem.headline: Unpredictable weather threatens U.S. shuttle launch.

text.p: NASA was keeping a close eye on a rare mid-summer cold front that could threaten its plans to launch the space shuttle Discovery this week, officials said on Tuesday.

Launch controllers said the countdown was proceeding smoothly for the shuttle's planned 10:41 a.m. EDT (1441 GMT) blast off on Thursday from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre. Only the weather appeared to pose a problem.
U.S. Air Force meteorologists said there was a 40 percent chance that a cold front moving through Florida would prevent the shuttle's launch because of low cloud and rain showers.
Forecasters said the unpredictable nature of the cold front, unusual for this time of year, was making their job difficult.
"We almost need to go to the Psychic Friends Network to determine just where the front's going to be," shuttle weather officer Ed Priselac told a news conference.
Afternoon thunderstorms may also delay the retraction of the shuttle's launch pad gantry on Wednesday, he added.
Discovery's 11-day mission has a wide-range of objectives. Soon after reaching orbit, the crew of six will release a German-built satellite for nine days of atmospheric research.
They also will watch Comet Hale-Bopp through a telescope as it departs the vicinity of the sun and test a 5-foot long Japanese robot arm intended for use on the planned International Space Station.
